prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength and opening the 10^-18 regime of frequency metrology

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as my single-part preference; my configuration is unchanged from round 1. Reading the full exchange, five of eight members name it first and all five give the same credit (Katori for the magic-wavelength concept and first strontium demonstration, Ye for taking the clock to about 1e-18), so the credit question is settled in a way it is not for B017, B033, B056 or B053. The chair asks what the citation recognises that 2005 and 2012 did not. My answer: the comb (Hall, Hansch) gave a way to count optical cycles, and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) honoured control of single ions and photons; neither prize contains the idea of interrogating a large ensemble of neutral atoms in a lattice with the light shift cancelled, which trades single-ion isolation for statistical power and gives stability and accuracy no single-ion clock can match. That is an invention with an identifiable date and author, which fits the 'discovery or invention' criterion and the aim of naming the topic and the people responsible for the original work. It is reproduced at many national laboratories and already used for relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants, so maturity is not in doubt.
statement.case_against: The novelty reservation is shared by every supporter, me included, and I do not think it is fully removable: a sceptic can still read lattice clocks as the next step on a line already honoured twice. The citation must therefore name the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice and not 'precision metrology'. Second, the redefinition of the second has not happened; I do not regard it as a precondition, since the prize is for the demonstrated invention and performance, but it means the largest practical consequence is still prospective. Third, a two-name credit omits Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow and Derevianko. I think that is defensible because Katori proposed and first demonstrated the scheme and Ye led the accuracy frontier, but it is a real judgement and the omitted names should be recorded. Finally, I still cannot assess B055 neutrally, so I leave it out of my configuration and out of my alternatives for this round.

responses.point: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the cleanest theory-plus-experiment pairing, with a quantitative 2011 prediction followed by the 2018 discovery, and a trio with no obvious omission among the supplied names.
responses.response: The prediction-then-discovery structure is what I find most attractive in B038, and I keep it as my first alternative. But your own case_against names an eight-year-old field and a disputed origin of superconductivity, and I weigh those more heavily than you do. I would want a citation that stays on flat bands and correlated insulators without implying a mechanism, and I would want to see the pairing question narrowed before putting it ahead of a settled invention. On your trio, I am not convinced it is as clean as you say: Mehlig notes that Cao and the other early authors stand outside it, so it is no cleaner than the clock credit, which I find tighter.

responses.point: B038 has the broadest opening support, and if the committee values maturity above breadth, optical lattice clocks are the safer choice.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of your argument and take your last sentence as a fair summary of why I land on B002: it is the safer choice and I do value maturity here. You also ask for a citation that does not claim to explain superconductivity, which I support. What would move me toward B038 is a clear experimental credit rule that handles Cao and the first-author group, and a few more years in which the correlated phases are shown to be understood. Breadth of opening support, which you cite, was real, but the round-1 statements show it was mostly second-place support from members who also judge it early.

responses.point: The experimental Higgs discovery is mature and unrecognised on the experimental side, but attribution under three names is the decisive weakness, and B002 or B038 are better-attributed alternatives.
responses.response: I accept the scientific case and I note that you yourself list B002 first among your alternatives, which I read as a genuine bridge between us. Where I differ is that I see no principled rule yet for three names: founding spokespeople, discovery-year spokespeople and analysis conveners each give a different trio, and a prize that picks among them looks like a judgement about leadership rather than discovery. Unless the committee can name a rule in this round, I cannot support B053 as a prize part, though I would not object to it being the subject of a later year's work.

responses.point: The strongest reservation on lattice clocks is cumulative recognition (2005, 2012), and the redefinition of the second has not happened, with credit beyond the two names not fully resolved.
responses.response: I share all three reservations and answer them as follows. On the 2005 and 2012 prizes, the distinctive element is the magic-wavelength neutral-atom lattice, and I would build the citation on it. On the second, I would not wait, given that 10^-18 performance has been reproduced independently. On credit, Katori and Ye are defensible. Regarding your possible connection to the Hall laboratory, I think it is correctly recorded as a perceived link rather than a conflict, since you are not close to the credited names now; I would record it and not require abstention, and I note that B002 would still lead without your voice, which is the more reassuring test.

responses.point: Circuit QED is the architecture of superconducting quantum processors, with a three-person split of Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Girvin.
responses.response: I understand the scientific weight of B017. I keep my position, as I did in round 1: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits is recent, and leaving out Blais, who proposed the 2004 scheme, is difficult to defend for a proposal-plus-experiment prize. I would also ask you to keep your recusal statement on record for B017, given your directorship of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, though I note that you now state B002 as your first preference, so this does not affect your ballot on the preferred part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes; I think yes, but others weigh this differently.
Whether omitting Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow and Derevianko from the credit is acceptable; I regard Katori and Ye as defensible but not beyond dispute.
Whether magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene becomes mature enough in a few years to rise above clocks; I cannot judge the pairing question from my own field.
Whether any principled credit rule exists for large-collaboration cases such as B053 and B043 under the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: I continue to disclose that I work in the transmission electron microscopy community with Chalmers colleagues and co-authors, and I would recuse myself from any decision on B055 (spherical-aberration correction), which I do not propose in my configuration or alternatives. Göran Johansson is also at Chalmers, which should be noted for circuit QED (B017). My profile shows no documented connection to Katori, Ye or other credited names on the shortlisted candidates, including B038 and B015. I also note Kroll's disclosed link to Hall's laboratory and treat it as a perceived connection to be recorded.
